title: How to Start Farming in the Philippines With Little or No Experience
metaTitle: Start Farming With No Experience: A Philippine Guide
metaDescription: Want to start farming with no experience? Learn free through the ATI, register in the RSBSA, start small, plan your first season and find starter loans.
keywords: how to start farming in the Philippines
excerpt: You can start farming with no experience if you learn first, start small and plan every step before you plant. Take free courses from the Agricultural Training Institute, register in the RSBSA so you qualify for DA help, and grow one crop on a small plot in your first season. anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, helps you plan that first season: it dates every task from your planting day and shows what your crop needs at each stage.

blocks.text:
Many new farmers in the Philippines are not new to hard work. They are OFWs coming home, office workers with family land, or young people who grew up near the bukid but never ran a season. You can learn the skills. What hurts beginners most is money spent before the lessons.

So the order matters. Learn, register, plan, then plant, and keep the first season small enough that a mistake does not end your farming.

items: Learn before you buy: the ATI offers free online courses, radio lessons and a contact center for farm questions.
Register in the RSBSA. It is free, it is for life, and it opens DA loans, insurance, seeds, fertilizer and soil analysis.
Start with one crop on a small plot, and know who will buy it before you plant.
Young farmers aged 18 to 30 may qualify for the ACPC KAYA loan of up to PHP 500,000 with no interest and no collateral.

blocks.text: What do you need to start farming?
Before you think about seeds, answer six questions. If one answer is missing, fix it first. It is cheaper than learning it in the field.

blocks.caption: Six things to sort out before your first season

blocks.text: How do you start farming step by step?

items.title: Learn the basics
items.text: Take a free online course from the ATI, or read the PhilRice PalayCheck system if you plan to grow palay. Spend a few days with an experienced farmer during planting and harvest.

items.title: Register in the RSBSA
items.text: Get the form from your city or municipal agriculture office. Bring a valid ID and proof of ownership, tenancy or lease if you farm your own lot. The DA says registration is free and lasts for life.

items.title: Know your land
items.text: Walk the lot after heavy rain to see where water stays. Ask the agriculture office about soil analysis, one of the services open to RSBSA farmers.

items.title: Choose one crop
items.text: Pick a crop that suits your land, your water and a buyer near you. Our guides to [what crop to plant this season](/blog/what-crop-to-plant-this-season) and [small farm ideas](/blog/small-farm-ideas-philippines) can help.

items.title: Pick the planting date
items.text: Plant so the crop avoids the worst of the weather at flowering and harvest. See the [best time to plant rice](/blog/best-time-to-plant-rice-philippines) for palay.

items.title: Write the season plan and budget
items.text: List every task from land preparation to harvest, with its day and its cost. A loan officer will ask for a farm plan and budget too.

items.title: Start small
items.text: Plant a part of your land first. Learn the crop, then grow the area next season.

items.title: Keep records from day one
items.text: Write what you did, what it cost and what you harvested. Your second season starts from those notes.

blocks.text: Where can beginners learn farming for free?
You do not need to pay for a seminar to start farming well. The government already offers a lot for free, and much of it works from a phone.

items: **ATI e Learning**: self paced online certificate courses on crops, livestock and poultry, fisheries and sustainable agriculture.
**School on the Air**: farm lessons by radio, made for farmers in hard to reach areas.
**Farmers' Contact Center**: the ATI help desk for farm questions, by call, text, email or online chat.
**PalayCheck**: the PhilRice rice crop management system, with key checks for each stage, in English and in Tagalog.
**Other farmers**: ask in the [farmer community](/features/farmer-community) of anee.io, and work beside a neighbor for a season.

blocks.text: How much money do you need to start farming?

It depends on the crop, the land and the area. A hectare of palay costs far more than a small vegetable plot, and rented land adds its own cost. So do not trust a single number from a post. Instead, list every input and every work day, price them in your town, and add them up. Our guide to the [cost of producing rice per hectare](/blog/cost-of-producing-rice-per-hectare) shows the method.

If you need capital, the Agricultural Credit Policy Council has two programs worth knowing. Both lend through partner cooperatives and rural banks, and both ask for proof of registration, such as the RSBSA.

blocks.text: Applicants sign up through the ACPC online portal and go through a program briefing. KAYA asks for a simple business plan, and ANYO asks individuals for a farm plan and budget. A dated season plan makes both much easier to write.
What mistakes do first time farmers make?

items: Planting the whole land in the first season, then running out of cash halfway.
Planting without a buyer, then selling at any price at harvest.
Buying chemicals because of an ad, without knowing the problem or the active ingredient.
Forgetting to count labor, including their own days.
Keeping no records, so the second season repeats the first season's mistakes.

blocks.title: Do not spray what you cannot name
blocks.text: Before you buy any pesticide, find out what the problem is. Then choose by active ingredient, and follow the product label and its FPA registration. Ask your municipal agriculturist if you are unsure.
How can anee.io help you start farming?

A beginner's biggest gap is knowing what to do next, and when. anee.io fills that gap with dates. On the free Libre plan, the [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar) dates every task from your planting day. Each lot also shows its growth stage, what to do now and what to watch for. Notes and photos keep your record as you go.

blocks.label: Start free

items.q: Can I start farming with no experience?
items.a: Yes, if you learn first and start small. Take a free ATI course, work beside an experienced farmer, and grow one crop on part of your land in your first season. Keep records so you learn faster.

items.q: What is the easiest crop to start farming with?
items.a: Fast leafy vegetables are a common start, because a mistake costs little and you learn quickly. The ATI says pechay can be harvested 30 to 40 days after sowing. Choose a crop that someone near you will buy.

items.q: Do I need to register as a farmer?
items.a: It is not required to farm, but RSBSA registration is free and opens DA help. The DA lists loans, crop and livestock insurance, seeds, fertilizer, technical help and soil analysis for registered farmers.

items.q: Is there a loan for young farmers in the Philippines?
items.a: Yes. The ACPC KAYA program lends up to PHP 500,000 to farm entrepreneurs aged 18 to 30, at 0 percent interest and with no collateral. A partner lender may charge a service fee of up to 3.5 percent.

items.q: Can an app teach me to farm?
items.a: An app cannot replace time in the field, but it can tell you what to do and when. anee.io dates every task from your planting day and shows your crop's stage, and Anee answers your questions in Tagalog or English.
